The one thing nobody else has

A black diamond is a lump of coal.

The town was named for the seams under it. So was the bakery — and the fire has never left the building.

The fire is built right on the floor of the oven. When the brick has taken enough heat the coals are raked out, the loaves go in on a long wooden peel, and the bricks do the rest of the work on their own.

That is the whole trick, and it hasn't changed in a hundred and twenty-four years. It's also why there used to be a sign on the door by noon: the bread was gone.

Four things under one roof

A bakery that grew a restaurant around itself.

It started as a bakehouse with one oven. A deli wing went on in 1989, breakfast started in 1991, and the coffee shop followed in 1994. Same building, same oven.

The brick oven

Hearth loaves are still baked on the floor of the oven Bill Hadley built — whole wheat, sourdough, rye, and the potato-flour Crystal Mountain the town buys by the armload.

The bakery case

Pies, donuts, danish, bear claws, eclairs, macaroons, cinnamon rolls and frosted sugar cookies — all made here, and mostly gone by the afternoon.

Three meals a day

Eggs and hotcakes from seven in the morning, sandwiches built on the morning's hearth bread at midday, and a full dinner menu from four.

Cakes & the banquet room

Wedding cakes, round and sheet cakes and cupcakes are made to order, and there's a banquet room and catering for the rest of the party.

Inside the bakehouse

Where the morning happens.

Since Bill Hadley built it

Eight families have kept this oven lit.

Willard "Bill" Hadley built the bakery and its oven in 1902, on ground the Black Diamond Mining Company had bought from Ethan A. Scott eighteen years before.

His daughter Francys was born in the bakery in 1910. His father-in-law Fabro was listed as the baker on that year's census. By the twenties his son Emil was running the place, helped by his sister and his Aunt Ruby. The Eippers bought it from the coal company in 1944; it passed to James Leroy, then F. A. Dawson, then Wallace Smith, then Doug Wieding in 1985.

Wieding added the deli wing on the south end in 1989, and the sandwiches took off because the bread had been baked that morning a few feet away. Breakfast started in December 1991. The coffee shop wing went on the north end in 1994, and an espresso bar, a gift shop and a banquet room followed. Insung Kang and Eunjeong Kim run it today, and the recipes have not moved.

Come by or call ahead

Reserve a table, order a cake, or just walk in.

  1. Walk in

    No reservation needed for breakfast or lunch. The bakery case is the first thing inside the door, and the counter runs on its own.

  2. Call for a table

    Dinner and larger parties are easiest by phone. The banquet room and catering are booked the same way.

  3. Start a cake

    Wedding, round and sheet cakes and cupcakes are all made here to order — a phone call starts one.
